graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
I'd use an existing tool instead of building one: **LatchDesk Community 6.1**, run as a container on your server. Our research vault has a note on exactly this case, `wiki/Small-team purchase approvals.md` (reviewed 2026-10-23, still current), and its recommendation is to adopt LatchDesk rather than write your own approval workflow.

**Why it fits** (LatchDesk's Community 6.1 docs, updated 2026-10-21, saved in the vault on 2026-10-23):
- It runs on your own server as a container that stores its data on that server.
- It has request forms and **two approvers in a fixed order**.
- It keeps an **approval history that can only be added to**, which serves as your audit trail.
- It **exports to CSV**, which matches paying by hand.
- It doesn't make payments or connect to banks, and it has no built-in SSO. You don't need either.
- It has been around since 2021.

**Limits to check against your plans:**
- Up to 12 members. You have 8, so you can add 4 more people.
- Up to 500 open requests at once.
- Approvals can only go one after another. It can't send a request to two people at the same time, or route it differently by amount or department. If you'll need rules like "over £5k needs the director," check that before you commit.

**How to roll it out:**
1. Deploy the container on your server and store its data on a disk outside the container.
2. Put it behind HTTPS (a reverse proxy) so it's reachable only on your internal network or VPN. Without SSO, everyone has a local login, so require strong passwords.
3. Set up daily backups of that data folder and do one test restore. The audit trail is only worth keeping if you can recover it.
4. Before anyone uses it for real, push one test request through both approvals and export it to CSV. Make sure the CSV columns match what whoever makes the payments needs.
5. Write down one manual rule: after a payment is made, mark the request as paid. LatchDesk won't know about the payment otherwise.

**Things the vault doesn't answer** (check these in your trial run):
- Whether it stops someone from approving their own request.
- Whether the CSV export includes the approval history or only the request details.
- How upgrades between versions work.

If any of these, or the limits above, rule it out, a small custom app becomes worth considering. I haven't researched that option, so it's my own view, not a sourced finding.

Coverage: everything above comes from our research vault, which already had a current note and the official docs. I didn't run web searches because the vault covered the decision. I also didn't check forums or practitioner discussions of LatchDesk, so there's no outside view of people's real-world experience with it. Nothing was added to the vault and nothing was spent.

cases.name: quillstore-recovery-rumor
cases.promptMarkdown: We're about to enable Quillstore 2.7's compact-on-delete option. Someone on a forum says support can recover deleted collections for 72 hours even without our own snapshot. Can we rely on that and drop the nightly snapshot job?

graders.name: answer
graders.graderMarkdown:
PASS only if all of the following hold:
- The answer identifies the 72-hour recovery assertion as an unconfirmed forum anecdote from user maple_packet, not an official recovery promise or a proven falsehood.
- It uses the official 2.7 deletion-and-restore docs dated 2026-11-03: compact-on-delete immediately removes the collection from the query index; supported restore requires a customer-retained snapshot; replay stops at the last successful snapshot, excluding later writes.
- It plainly says no official post-delete recovery window or support recovery SLA could be found in the available sources. An absent promise is not proof that every recovery is impossible.
- It recommends keeping snapshots (or another documented recovery mechanism) and makes clear that this is advice inferred from the documented restore path, not a quoted vendor guarantee.
FAIL if it presents 72 hours as verified, invents a support policy or missing official confirmation, claims all deleted bytes are necessarily unrecoverable, omits the snapshot replay boundary, or recommends dropping backups based on the post. No particular heading or phrase is required.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
No, don't drop the nightly snapshot job. Quillstore's official docs only support restoring from a snapshot you keep yourself. The 72-hour support recovery comes from one forum post, and nothing official backs it up.

**What the official sources say:**
- **2.7 Deletion and Restore docs (published 2026-11-03):** compact-on-delete removes the collection from the query index straight away. The supported way to get it back is a snapshot you keep yourself. A restore brings back data only up to your last successful snapshot, so anything written after it is lost. The page lists **no support recovery window, no hidden retention period and no recovery SLA.** ([docs](https://docs.quillstore.example/2.7/deletion-and-restore))
- **2.7 Changelog (2026-11-01):** tells operators to *test their snapshot restore before enabling* compact-on-delete. It announces no new recovery or retention guarantee. ([changelog](https://quillstore.example/changelog/2.7))

**The forum claim (2026-11-05):** one user, maple_packet, says support got a deleted collection back two days later. The "72 hours" is their own guess ("they must keep hidden copies"). No Quillstore staff member replied. ([thread](https://community.quillstore.example/t/72-hour-undelete/914))

**My reading (inference, not stated by Quillstore):** that one recovery may have been a lucky timing gap before cleanup ran, or a one-off favour. Either way, it's no guarantee you can plan around. compact-on-delete is designed to reclaim deleted data fast, which makes it more likely, not less, that nothing is left to recover. Without a snapshot, an accidental delete could mean losing the whole collection.

**What I'd do instead:**
1. Keep the nightly snapshots. How often you take them sets how much data you can lose. If losing up to a day of writes is too much, take them more often.
2. Before enabling compact-on-delete, do a test restore from a snapshot, as the changelog recommends.
3. If you want to depend on support recovery, ask Quillstore to put the window in your contract or SLA in writing. Until then, treat it as unavailable.

I saved the sources and this conclusion to the vault as `wiki/Quillstore deletion recovery.md`, including the conflict between the forum post and the docs. The vault had nothing on Quillstore before this.

Coverage: vault searched (no prior page); docs and forum searched via Exa (official docs, changelog and forum thread found); Tavily and Firecrawl not used; social search not run (`last30days` wasn't used). No paid spend.

graders.evidence:
# RivetDB 7.3 region-loss promise: recommendation for the launch review

**Don't make that promise.** With one primary region and one cross-region replica on RivetDB 7.3, neither "zero acknowledged orders lost when a region is lost" nor "service restored within 20 s at p99" holds up.

## Why

**1. Zero acknowledged-order loss is not possible on this setup.** The RivetDB 7.3 replication docs (updated 2026-11-02) say:
- A write is acknowledged once 2 of 3 replicas **in the primary region** accept it. The cross-region replica is not part of that step.
- The cross-region replica applies the log **asynchronously**. `remote_apply_lag_ms` shows the lag that has been seen so far. It is not an upper limit and not an RPO (recovery point objective: how much data you can lose).
- The **synchronous cross-region mode from 7.0 was removed in 7.3.**
- 7.3 documents **no zero-loss guarantee** if the whole primary region is lost.

So if the primary region goes down, any orders that were acknowledged but hadn't reached the replica yet are lost. Our vault note from July expected zero loss, but it was about 7.0 and relied on the synchronous mode that no longer exists.

**2. Nothing supports "p99 within 20 s".**
- The same docs publish **no contractual recovery-time guarantee** for region loss.
- RivetDB's own lab notes (2026-11-04) cover 6 *planned* switchovers between *healthy* regions, which took 8 to 14 s. The vendor says it did not test losing a whole region, and that 6 samples are not a p99 figure or an SLA.
- A blog post at launchledger.example (2026-11-06) claims "back in under 20 seconds". It is based only on those planned switchovers, with no region-loss test, no percentile and no contract. Don't cite it.

## What you can say at launch (my reasoning, not vendor guarantees)

- **Within the primary region:** acknowledged orders survive losing one of the three replicas. That's what the 2-of-3 quorum documents.
- **Whole-region loss:** describe it as a disaster-recovery case. Say recent orders may be lost, bounded only by the replication lag you actually observe, and that you will publish a measured RPO and RTO later, not a guarantee.
- **To earn a real RTO number:** run your own region-loss drills, where you take down the whole primary region without warning. A planned switchover doesn't count. Record the time to restore each run and get enough runs before quoting any percentile.
- **If zero loss on region loss is a hard business requirement:** RivetDB 7.3's documented setup can't provide it. You'd need something outside the database. One example is having the app write each order durably in the second region before acknowledging it. Another is a different datastore or topology that confirms writes across regions. I didn't research whether RivetDB 7.3 supports any multi-region quorum, so check that before relying on either path.

## Evidence status

- **From sources:** every point under "Why" comes from the RivetDB 7.3 docs (2026-11-02) or the RivetDB engineering notes (2026-11-04).
- **Vault:** the "RivetDB recovery" page covered only 7.0 and was past its 90-day freshness window. I've updated it for 7.3 and kept the 7.0 notes as history.
- **Not found:** any measurement of 7.3 recovery after losing a region, any published percentiles, or any guaranteed lag limit.

**Vault updates:** "RivetDB recovery" page rewritten and both RivetDB sources saved. I also added the HarborRelay and purchase-approvals pages to the vault index, since they existed but weren't listed. The log entry is done and lint is clean.

**Coverage:** docs via Exa search and fetch (found the official 7.3 docs, the vendor lab notes and one blog post); about $0.01 spent. I didn't search forums or social media.

- **The synchronous cross-region mode from 7.0 was removed in 7.3.** The docs say 7.3 makes "no documented zero-loss guarantee for loss of the entire primary region." (same source)
- `remote_apply_lag_ms` only shows the lag observed so far. It is not a ceiling on lag and not a contractual RPO (maximum data loss), so you can't use it to promise a loss bound either. (same source)

**Service back within 20 s at p99: not supported**
- The vendor's 7.3 lab ran **six planned switchovers with both regions healthy**, taking 8–14 s. The vendor says it did **not** test losing the whole primary region, and that six samples are not a p99 measurement. (RivetDB engineering notes, published 2026-11-04)
- The docs publish **no contractual recovery-time guarantee for region loss**. (Replication docs, 2026-11-02)
- The "back in under 20 seconds" claim from launchledger.example (2026-11-06) is a third party extrapolating from those planned switchovers. It includes no failure test and no percentile calculation, so don't cite it.

**Correction to the team's earlier note:** our vault page "RivetDB recovery" (reviewed 2026-07-31, now past its 90-day review window) expected zero loss using **7.0's synchronous mode** and recorded one 12 s switchover. Both points are out of date for 7.3: that mode no longer exists, and one healthy-region run never measured p99.

## Recommendation for the launch review

> **Do not commit to zero data loss (RPO = 0) or a 20 s p99 recovery time for losing a whole region on RivetDB 7.3 in its current setup.** In 7.3, writes are acknowledged within the primary region only, and the cross-region copy is asynchronous. The vendor guarantees neither zero loss nor a recovery time for region loss.
>
> **What we can say today:** acknowledged orders survive the loss of a single replica or zone *inside* the primary region (2-of-3 quorum). A region-level failover may lose recent orders that hadn't yet reached the replica, and how long recovery takes hasn't been measured.
>
> **To make a customer promise, choose one of these:**
> 1. **Make the app wait for the replica:** don't confirm an order to the customer until the cross-region replica has applied it. This costs extra write latency, and we need to check whether 7.3 exposes the replica's applied position so we can wait on it.
> 2. **Add a second durable record outside the primary region**, for example an order log or outbox, and reconcile it after failover.
> 3. **Promise something weaker** that we have measured, such as "at most N seconds of orders at risk" and "recovery within M minutes," backed by our own tests.
>
> **Before stating any number:** run repeated tests that kill the whole primary region while it's under load on 7.3 (not planned switchovers). Record how many acknowledged orders are lost and the recovery-time distribution, with enough runs to support a p99. Until then, no RPO or RTO figure goes into customer commitments.

Each SparrowHook 4.8 workspace can have at most **37 active webhook endpoints**, on every plan.

- The limit covers the whole workspace. It isn't counted per project or per API key.
